propositions.text: Rose-Marie Sahadeo seeks judicial review of a Board decision addressing her grievances about disciplinary measures and termination during CBSA training.
propositions.quote: Rose-Marie Sahadeo seeks judicial review of a decision of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations and Employment Board (the Board). That decision (2024 FPSLREB 12, the Decision) addressed a number of grievances by Ms. Sahadeo concerning several disciplinary measures taken against her, as well as the termination of her employment, during her training under the Officer Induction Development Program (OIDP) to become a Canadian Border Services Agency (CBSA) officer.

propositions.text: The Board also addressed grievances alleging discrimination, breach of management-rights clause, and disguised discipline.
propositions.quote: The Board also addressed grievances by Ms. Sahadeo alleging (i) discrimination based on gender and colour, (ii) a breach of the management-rights clause of the relevant collective agreement, and (iii) that she was subjected to disguised discipline.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that Ms. Sahadeo seeks judicial review of the Board's decision on her disciplinary and termination grievances and other allegations.

propositions.text: The Board allowed grievances on disciplinary measures and termination, reducing or setting aside suspensions and reinstating Ms. Sahadeo with three months salary and benefits.
propositions.quote: The grievances concerning disciplinary measures and her termination were allowed, in whole or in part, and the other grievances were denied. The disciplinary measures involved suspensions of various durations. The suspensions were all either reduced or set aside. The termination was set aside, and the Board awarded Ms. Sahadeo three months of salary and benefits (to reflect the finding that, at the time of her termination, she had three months left in the OIDP and should have been allowed to complete them). The Board determined that Ms. Sahadeo should be reinstated at the beginning of the OIDP.

paragraphs.summary: The Board allowed some grievances, denied others, set aside suspensions and termination, awarded three months pay, and reinstated Ms. Sahadeo at OIDP start.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo argues she should have full retroactive salary and benefits, reinstatement at her training stage, and that the Board erred denying discrimination grievance.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo takes issue with the Decision in three respects. First, she argues that she should have been awarded full salary and benefits retroactive to the date of her termination, a period of many years, instead of just three months. Second, she argues that she should have been reinstated at the stage of her training that she had reached when she was terminated, and not at the beginning. Third, Ms. Sahadeo argues that the Board erred in denying her grievance based on discrimination.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Sahadeo argues for full retroactive pay, reinstatement at her training stage, and that the Board erred on discrimination grievance denial.

propositions.text: The parties agree and the court concurs that the standard of review is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The parties agree that the standard of review applicable to all the issues Ms. Sahadeo raises is reasonableness. I concur.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties agree and it concurs that reasonableness is the standard of review.

propositions.text: Vavilov guides that reasonableness review focuses on decision and reasoning, requiring justification, transparency, and intelligibility.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada provided considerable assistance in assessing reasonableness in its decision in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 65 (Vavilov). Some of the Supreme Court’s guidance in Vavilov is particularly applicable in this case: At paragraph 83: [T]he focus of reasonableness review must be on the decision actually made by the decision maker, including both the decision maker’s reasoning process and the outcome. At paragraph 86, citing Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 190 at para. 47: Reasonableness … “is concerned mostly with the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process”, as well as “with whether the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law” … [I]t is not enough for the outcome of a decision to be justifiable. Where reasons for a decision are required, the decision must also be justified, by way of those reasons. [emphasis in original] At paragraph 96: [I]t is not ordinarily appropriate for the reviewing court to fashion its own reasons in order to buttress the administrative decision. Even if the outcome of the decision could be reasonable under different circumstances, it is not open to a reviewing court to disregard the flawed basis for a decision and substitute its own justification for the outcome. At paragraph 103: A decision will be unreasonable if the reasons for it (i) “read holistically, fail to reveal a rational chain of analysis”, or (ii) “read in conjunction with the record do not make it possible to understand the decision maker’s reasoning on a critical point”. At paragraph 131: Whether a particular decision is consistent with the administrative body’s past decisions is … a constraint that the reviewing court should consider when determining whether an administrative decision is reasonable. Where a decision maker does depart from longstanding practices or established internal authority, it bears the justificatory burden of explaining that departure in its reasons. If the decision maker does not satisfy this burden, the decision will be unreasonable. [emphasis in original] At paragraph 133: Where the impact of a decision on an individual’s rights and interests is severe, the reasons provided to that individual must reflect the stakes. … [I]f a decision has particularly harsh consequences for the affected individual, the decision maker must explain why its decision best reflects the legislature’s intention. This includes decisions with consequences that threaten an individual’s life, liberty, dignity or livelihood.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Vavilov for reasonableness review principles emphasizing justification, transparency, and explanation of departures from practice.

propositions.text: The Board found Ms. Sahadeo's termination for unsatisfactory performance unreasonable and reinstated her under section 230 of the Public Sector Labour Relations Act.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo was reinstated because the Board, pursuant to its authority under section 230 of the Public Sector Labour Relations Act, S.C. 2003, c. 22, found that the termination of her employment for unsatisfactory performance under paragraph 12(1)(d) of the Financial Administration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-11, was unreasonable. This aspect of the Decision is not in issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Board found the termination unreasonable and reinstated Ms. Sahadeo; this is not contested.

propositions.text: The Board awarded only three months pay and benefits, tied to remaining training time, recognizing it could not promote Ms. Sahadeo and no guarantee of training success.
propositions.quote: However, the Board did not reinstate Ms. Sahadeo with full pay and benefits retroactive to the date of her dismissal. Instead, it awarded her only three months of pay and benefits on the basis that this reflected the amount of time that was left in her training. The Board recognized that it did not have the power to give Ms. Sahadeo the promotion to Border Services Officer (BSO) that she had been seeking in her training and was limited to putting her in the position she would have been but for her improper termination. The Board also recognized that there was no guarantee that Ms. Sahadeo would complete her training successfully.

paragraphs.summary: The Board limited pay to three months, reflecting remaining training, noting it could not promote her and training success was uncertain.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo argues usual practice awards full back pay retroactive to dismissal, including for probationary employees, citing Bahniuk, Bergey, Alexis, and Dhaliwal.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo argues that the usual practice in a case of unjust dismissal is to reinstate the employee with compensation for losses from the date of dismissal until the date of reinstatement: Bahniuk v. Canada (Attorney General), 2016 FCA 127, [2016] F.C.J. No. 467 at para. 22 (Bahniuk); Bergey v. Canada (Attorney General), 2017 FCA 30, [2017] F.C.J. No. 142 at para. 36 (Bergey). Ms. Sahadeo adds that this approach extends to probationary employees: Alexis v. Deputy Head (Royal Canadian Mounted Police), 2020 FPSLREB 9, aff’d 2021 FCA 216; Dhaliwal v. Treasury Board (Solicitor General Canada - Correctional Service), 2004 PSSRB 109. Ms. Sahadeo argues therefore that the fact that she was in training was not itself a basis to deny her full retroactive pay and benefits. As noted above, the standard of reasonableness requires that a tribunal explain itself if it strays from normal practice.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Sahadeo argues usual practice awards full retroactive pay, including for probationary employees, and training status is no basis to deny it.

propositions.text: The Crown argues the Board reasonably awarded three months pay; full back pay is common but not default; Bahniuk involved compensation in lieu.
propositions.quote: The respondent, the Attorney General of Canada (the Crown), argues that it was open to the Board to reinstate Ms. Sahadeo with three months’ pay and benefits, and that the standard of reasonableness calls for considerable deference on remedy. The Crown argues that Bahniuk describes reinstatement with full back pay and benefits as a common outcome, but not a default outcome. The Crown notes that Bahniuk itself involved compensation in lieu reinstatement, and therefore did not award full back pay.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the Board reasonably awarded three months pay; full back pay is common but not default; Bahniuk involved compensation in lieu.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo replies Bahniuk is distinguishable as forward-looking, unlike this rearward-looking case, citing Bergey.
propositions.quote: In reply, Ms. Sahadeo notes that the factual circumstances in Bahniuk are distinguishable from the present case because it was forward-looking (determining compensation in lieu reinstatement) whereas the present case is rearward-looking (seeking to make the applicant whole for her losses in the past). She notes that this distinction between these two types of circumstances is mentioned in Bergey at paragraph 36.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Sahadeo replies Bahniuk is distinguishable as forward-looking, unlike this rearward-looking case, citing Bergey.

propositions.text: The court agrees the Board had broad remedial power and should not be lightly interfered with; Bahniuk involved dismissal for cause unlike here.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Crown that the Board had a broad power to craft a remedy in Ms. Sahadeo’s case, and that this Court should not lightly interfere with the Board’s approach. I note also that the facts in the present case may be distinguishable from those in Bahniuk since the latter case concerned dismissal for cause rather than for unsatisfactory performance.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the Board had broad remedial power and should not be lightly interfered with; Bahniuk involved dismissal for cause unlike here.

propositions.text: The Board failed to adequately explain limiting pay to three months versus almost eight years; reasoning is brief and quoted.
propositions.quote: That said, I find that the Board failed to adequately explain why it limited its pay and benefits award to three months following Ms. Sahadeo’s dismissal versus almost eight years. The Board’s reasoning in this regard is brief. It is found in paragraphs 448 and 449 of the Decision, as reproduced here: [448] If the employer had provided an additional three months of assessment, as was allowed under the OIDP, rather than terminating her employment, the grievor would have received three-months of pay and benefits prior to a determination by the employer of whether she met the requirements for promotion to FB-03. I therefore order the payment of three-months of pay and benefits at the applicable rate of pay at the time of the termination of employment, to make her whole. [449] My jurisdiction is limited to reinstating the grievor to the OIDP and to putting her in the position she would have been, but for the employer's unreasonable assessment. I have found that there were two periods of assessment where the grievor did not receive a reasonable assessment due to either bad faith or a failure to provide sufficient time for an appropriate assessment. I find, therefore, that to make the grievor whole, the only option is for her to start the OIDP from the beginning.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board inadequately explained limiting pay to three months versus eight years, quoting the brief reasoning.

propositions.text: The Board tied back pay to remaining training, recognized no promotion power, but did not explain why more pay was denied or that training success uncertainty influenced award.
propositions.quote: The Board seems to have tied the three months of back pay to the time that would have remained in Ms. Sahadeo’s training if she had not been unjustly dismissed. It was conscious that it could not award her the promotion to BSO that she had been seeking. However, the Board did not adequately explain why it decided that Ms. Sahadeo was not entitled to an award of back pay and benefits greater than three months. The Board may have been disinclined to award more back pay because of the very real possibility that Ms. Sahadeo would never be successful in her training, but it did not say so in the Decision. Moreover, the Board appears to have been of the view that the award of three months of back pay and benefits would make Ms. Sahadeo whole as compensation for the unreasonable assessment that led to her dismissal. However, this view is not justified.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board tied pay to training time but failed to explain denial of more pay or training success concerns.

propositions.text: The Board's limitation of compensation award was unreasonable given its conclusion of improper termination.
propositions.quote: In view of the Board’s conclusion that Ms. Sahadeo’s termination was improper, I do not understand the reasoning that led it to limit its compensation award as it did. In my view, this aspect of the Decision was unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board's limitation of compensation unreasonable given its finding of improper termination.

propositions.text: The Board was not obliged to award full back pay but failed to explain why it did not; issue remitted for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: That said, I am not convinced that the only conclusion open to the Board was to award full back pay and benefits retroactive to the date of her termination. In my view, one of the Board’s tasks was to determine the proper compensation for Ms. Sahadeo’s unjust dismissal, and it was not obliged to award full pay and benefits back to the date of termination. The Board’s failure was in not explaining adequately why it chose not to. I would remit this issue to the Board for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds the Board was not obliged to award full back pay but must explain why not; remits issue for reconsideration.

propositions.text: The Board ruled Ms. Sahadeo should be reinstated at the beginning of OIDP.
propositions.quote: As indicated in paragraph 449 of the Decision (quoted at paragraph 12 above), the Board ruled that Ms. Sahadeo should be reinstated at the beginning of the OIDP. Ms. Sahadeo argues that this conclusion was also unreasonable and that she should have been reinstated at the stage of her training that she had reached at the time of her termination, that is, three months from the end.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo argues she should be reinstated at her training stage, not at the beginning.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo argues that this conclusion was also unreasonable and that she should have been reinstated at the stage of her training that she had reached when she was terminated, that is, three months from the end.

paragraphs.summary: The Board ruled reinstatement at OIDP start; Ms. Sahadeo argues she should be reinstated at her training stage.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo has completed OIDP and is now a BSO; reinstatement stage issue is partly moot but relevant to service clock and finances.
propositions.quote: The Court was advised at the hearing of this application that Ms. Sahadeo has recently completed the OIDP successfully and is now a BSO. In light of this, Ms. Sahadeo, through her counsel, acknowledged that this aspect of her application is “a little bit moot almost”, in that it does not make sense now to return her to any particular stage of her training. That said, I agree with Ms. Sahadeo’s argument that the issue of the appropriate stage of training to which Ms. Sahadeo should have been returned may be relevant to her “service clock”, which could have important financial implications for her. In that sense, this issue is not moot.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Ms. Sahadeo completed OIDP; reinstatement stage is partly moot but relevant to service clock and finances.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Board's reinstatement at OIDP start was reasonable.
propositions.quote: As with the issue of proper compensation, it was the Board’s role to determine certain details of Ms. Sahadeo’s reinstatement. The question for this Court is whether the Board’s determination that Ms. Sahadeo should be reinstated at the beginning of the OIDP, instead of three months before the end, was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issue as whether the Board's reinstatement at OIDP start was reasonable.

propositions.text: The Board has expertise in reinstatement; it cannot promote; Ms. Sahadeo was absent almost eight years; success uncertain; Board found starting OIDP was only way to make whole.
propositions.quote: In considering this question, I have taken into account the following: The Board has expertise in respect of reinstatement of an employee after an unjust dismissal, including the details thereof. The Board was not empowered to promote Ms. Sahadeo and therefore could only reinstate her to the OIDP. Ms. Sahadeo was returned to training that was critical to her continued career progression after an absence of almost eight years (from her termination on May 1, 2016 to the Decision on January 25, 2024). Her success in completing the training was not at all certain. The Board concluded at paragraph 449 of the Decision that reinstating Ms. Sahadeo at the beginning of the OIDP was the only option that would make her whole. Though the Board did not discuss the point, the Crown notes that the passage of time without Ms. Sahadeo obtaining certification or field experience was such that restarting the OIDP at the beginning balanced fairness to her with the operational realities of law enforcement and the need to preserve public confidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Board's expertise, inability to promote, Ms. Sahadeo's long absence, uncertain success, and Board's conclusion that starting OIDP was only way to make whole.

propositions.text: The court acknowledges Ms. Sahadeo's argument that the Board did not express concern about her long absence and that courts should not add reasons to support decisions.
propositions.quote: With regard to the last of the foregoing points, I acknowledge Ms. Sahadeo’s argument that the Board did not express concern for the long period of time during which she was neither working as nor training to become a BSO, and that Vavilov instructs that a court in judicial review should not add reasons to those provided by the relevant decision maker in an effort to buttress its decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court acknowledges Ms. Sahadeo's argument that the Board did not express concern about her long absence and that courts should not add reasons to support decisions.

propositions.text: The Board's finding about restarting Ms. Sahadeo's training is unclear but relates to its limited jurisdiction to reinstate her to the OIDP.
propositions.quote: I acknowledge that the Board’s finding at paragraph 449 of the Decision that Ms. Sahadeo would be made whole by restarting her training from the beginning is not entirely clear. It appears to allude to the Board’s acknowledgement, earlier in the same paragraph, that its jurisdiction is limited to reinstating Ms. Sahadeo to the OIDP.

propositions.text: The Board had to decide at what stage of the OIDP Ms. Sahadeo should be reinstated.
propositions.quote: The Board had to decide at what stage of the OIDP she should be reinstated.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board's unclear finding about restarting training relates to its limited jurisdiction to reinstate Ms. Sahadeo to the OIDP and deciding the reinstatement stage.

propositions.text: The Board was concerned about Ms. Sahadeo's ability to complete training and saw restarting as the best remedy.
propositions.quote: I infer a concern by the Board, in light of the serious uncertainty about Ms. Sahadeo’s ability to complete the training with success, that the best remedy for all parties was for her to restart the training at the beginning.

propositions.text: The Board was aware of the time elapsed since termination and its effect on training value.
propositions.quote: The Board was certainly aware of the long passage of time since her termination and could not have been ignorant of the effect of time on the value of the training that Ms. Sahadeo had already undergone.

propositions.text: The Board's analysis meets the requirements for a reasonable decision under Vavilov.
propositions.quote: I understand that chain of analysis (even though it was not explicit), and I find that it meets the requirements for a reasonable decision as described in Vavilov.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board reasonably decided restarting training was best given uncertainty and time elapsed, meeting Vavilov standards.

propositions.text: The Board addressed and denied the discrimination grievance at paragraphs 458 to 487 of the Decision.
propositions.quote: The Board addressed the discrimination grievance at paragraphs 458 to 487 of the Decision and denied it.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Board denied the discrimination grievance in the Decision.

propositions.text: The discrimination grievance was based on the collective agreement's 'No Discrimination' clause prohibiting discrimination by gender and colour.
propositions.quote: The discrimination grievance was based on the “No Discrimination” clause of the applicable collective agreement, which prohibited discrimination based on gender and colour.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo is a black woman.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo is a black woman.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo cited belittling remarks, refusal to remove false sick leave allegation, unequal discipline, atypical termination announcement, and differential treatment as discrimination evidence.
propositions.quote: In support of her discrimination grievance, Ms. Sahadeo cited Belittling and derogatory remarks she had endured, The refusal to remove from her Training Performance Questionnaire a false allegation that she had abused sick leave, The unequal discipline imposed on her and a senior white male BSO following traveller allegations that both had behaved aggressively: Ms. Sahadeo received a 15-day suspension, while her colleague received no discipline, An announcement on the day of her termination advising all CBSA employees (and not just managers, as was the normal practice) that she was no longer an employee and should not be granted access to CBSA areas – this atypical announcement gave rise to many enquiries as to whether there were safety concerns, and Differential treatment she received as compared to other recruits, including less support and overly critical performance assessments.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes the discrimination grievance basis and Ms. Sahadeo's cited evidence of discrimination.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo acknowledges the Board applied the correct legal test requiring a prima facie case of discrimination with three elements.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo acknowledges that the Board applied the correct legal test on this issue, which required her to establish a prima facie case of discrimination by demonstrating, on a balance of probabilities, that (i) she has a protected characteristic, (ii) she experienced an adverse impact, and (iii) the protected characteristic was a factor in the adverse impact.

propositions.text: The Board recognized it was unnecessary to prove employer intent and must examine all circumstances including circumstantial evidence for subtle discrimination.
propositions.quote: The Board also recognized in paragraph 475 of the Decision that it was not necessary for Ms. Sahadeo to prove that her employer intended to discriminate, and that the Board’s role was to examine all the circumstances, including circumstantial evidence, to determine if there was the subtle scent of discrimination.

propositions.text: Mere suspicions of discrimination are insufficient.
propositions.quote: That said, the Board noted that mere suspicions of discrimination are not sufficient.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant agrees the Board applied the correct legal test requiring a prima facie case and recognized circumstantial evidence but not mere suspicion suffices.

propositions.text: The Board found Ms. Sahadeo met the first two prima facie discrimination elements but failed the third.
propositions.quote: The Board accepted that Ms. Sahadeo met the first two requirements for a prima facie case of discrimination but concluded that she failed to meet the third.

propositions.text: The Board considered each allegation and concluded none established a prima facie case of discrimination.
propositions.quote: The Board considered each of Ms. Sahadeo’s allegations and concluded that none established a prima facie case of discrimination.

paragraphs.summary: The Board found Ms. Sahadeo met two prima facie elements but failed the third and rejected all allegations as discrimination.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo argues the Board improperly excluded unequal discipline from its discrimination assessment.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo argues that the Board improperly excluded the inequality of discipline imposed on her and her senior white male colleague (see paragraph 24(C) above) from its assessment of her discrimination grievance.

propositions.text: The Board found the 15-day suspension grievance did not allege discrimination and thus excluded it from the discrimination grievance.
propositions.quote: The Board acknowledged Ms. Sahadeo's reliance on this unequal discipline, but stated as follows at paragraph 467 of the Decision: In her grievance against the 15-day suspension [related to the incident giving rise to the complaint of unequal discipline], the grievor did not allege a breach of the CHRA [Canadian Human Rights Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6]. The grievor had an opportunity to allege discrimination in this grievance but did not do so. I therefore find that her discrimination grievance does not include this disciplinary action of the employer.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the Board wrongly excluded unequal discipline from discrimination analysis; the Board found no discrimination claim in the suspension grievance.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo argues discrimination was implicit in her unequal discipline complaint and cites Parry Sound to say grievance formality should not bar consideration.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo argues that discrimination was an implicit aspect of her complaint of unequal discipline. She notes that the Board had already concluded at paragraph 466 of the Decision that the parts of her discrimination grievance relating to targeting by local managers, being singled out for different treatment and the employer’s failure to provide a respectful workplace, concerned continuous allegations. Therefore, Ms. Sahadeo argues, allegations of these kinds (which encompass the complaint of unequal discipline) were already included in her discrimination grievance by implication, and it was not necessary for her to make explicit mention of discrimination. She cites the statement in Parry Sound (District) Social Services Administration Board v. O.P.S.E.U., Local 324, 2003 SCC 42, [2003] 2 S.C.R. 157 at para. 68 (Parry Sound), to the effect that a grievance should not be won or lost on the technicality of form and argues that the Board erred in excluding this allegation from its discrimination analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues discrimination was implicit in her complaint and cites Parry Sound to oppose exclusion on technicality grounds.

propositions.text: The Board reasonably inferred discrimination was not contemplated in the suspension grievance due to lack of mention, consistent with Vavilov.
propositions.quote: In my view, and despite Parry Sound, it was open to the Board to infer as it did from the fact that Ms. Sahadeo’s grievance concerning her 15-day suspension did not mention discrimination, that discrimination was not contemplated at the time, or at least that it was not so serious as to merit mention. The Board’s finding in that regard does not fall afoul of the Supreme Court’s guidance in Vavilov.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board reasonably inferred no discrimination claim in the suspension grievance, consistent with Vavilov.

propositions.text: The Board considered the unequal discipline circumstances and reached a conclusion; the court cannot substitute its own.
propositions.quote: I agree with Ms. Sahadeo that the circumstances surrounding the complaint of unequal discipline were of concern and merited close examination by the Board. But the Board did consider those circumstances, and it reached a conclusion. For me to find the Board’s analysis unreasonable, I would have to reach my own conclusion on the evidence, which I am not permitted to do.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the Board considered unequal discipline but cannot replace the Board's conclusion with its own.

propositions.text: Ms. Sahadeo argues the Board failed to consider her incidents as a whole, addressing them only individually.
propositions.quote: Ms. Sahadeo also argues that, though the Board considered each of the specific incidents that she brought to its attention, it addressed them individually; it failed to consider them as a whole as it was required to do.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the Board failed to consider all incidents together as required.

propositions.text: The Board cited Turner for the requirement to consider all circumstantial evidence and infer discrimination if more probable than other explanations.
propositions.quote: Again, I disagree. The Board at paragraph 477 of the Decision cited explicitly the following guidance from Turner v. Canada Border Services Agency, 2020 CHRT 1 at para. 54: … The Tribunal is tasked with discerning whether discrimination was a factor in failure to hire. To do so the Tribunal must consider all of the circumstantial evidence, make findings of fact and determine whether the inference that may be drawn from the facts support [sic] a finding of discrimination on the balance of probabilities. However, there has to be a nexus between the conduct under scrutiny and a prohibited ground of discrimination. The nexus can be inferred through the circumstantial evidence, but the inference of discrimination must be more probable than other possible inferences. In making the inference, the fact at issue must be proved by other facts. Each piece of evidence need not alone lead to the conclusion. The pieces of evidence, each by themselves insufficient, are combined to provide a basis for the inference that the fact at issue exists. … [emphasis added]

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board cited Turner requiring consideration of all evidence and inference of discrimination if more probable.

propositions.text: Though not explicit, the Board recognized its obligation to consider all allegations as a whole and assessed each allegation.
propositions.quote: It is true that the Board did not explicitly state that it had considered all of Ms. Sahadeo’s allegations as a whole, but the Decision demonstrates that it assessed each allegation and recognized its obligation to consider them as a whole.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Board recognized and fulfilled its obligation to consider all allegations as a whole.

propositions.text: The evidence was not compelling enough to find the Board's failure to explicitly discuss all evidence together unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the evidence of discrimination was not so compelling that I am led to conclude that the Board’s failure to discuss explicitly the whole of such evidence together, distinct from each separate incident, rendered the Decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: To conclude otherwise would require the court to reach its own conclusions on the evidence, which it cannot do.
propositions.quote: In my view, to conclude otherwise would require me to reach my own conclusions on the evidence which, as I have indicated above, I am not permitted to do.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the evidence insufficient to deem the Board's failure to discuss all evidence together unreasonable and cannot substitute its own conclusions.

propositions.text: The court concludes the Board's analysis of the discrimination grievance was reasonable.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the Board’s analysis of the discrimination grievance was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Board's discrimination grievance analysis was reasonable.

propositions.text: The court grants the judicial review application in part, setting aside paragraph 495 on salary and benefits and remitting it to the Board.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out above, I would grant the present application for judicial review in part. I would set aside paragraph 495 of the Decision concerning the award of salary and benefits and remit that aspect to the Board for reconsideration.

propositions.text: The court dismisses the application in all other respects.
propositions.quote: I would otherwise dismiss the application.

paragraphs.summary: The court partially grants judicial review, setting aside salary award paragraph and remitting it, dismissing other claims.

propositions.text: The court awards Ms. Sahadeo costs of $2500 due to her substantial financial success on the application.
propositions.quote: Because my proposed disposition of this application may give Ms. Sahadeo substantial success, at least from a financial viewpoint, though not on other points, I would award her costs in the all-inclusive amount of $2500.

paragraphs.summary: The court awards Ms. Sahadeo costs of $2500 for her partial financial success.

propositions.text: The respondent requests to amend the style of cause to identify the Attorney General of Canada as sole respondent; Ms. Sahadeo does not object.
propositions.quote: Finally, the respondent requests, and Ms. Sahadeo does not object, that the style of cause be amended to identify the Attorney General of Canada as the sole respondent.

propositions.text: The court grants the request and amends the style of cause accordingly.
propositions.quote: I would grant that request. I would amend the style of cause as shown at the beginning of these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent requests and the court grants amending the style of cause to name Attorney General as sole respondent.
